catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbacy-nulliu: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on the abbacy nullius of Wettingen-Mehrerau describes a Cistercian abbey near Bregenz in Austria. Wettingen itself was founded in Switzerland in 1227 by Henry of Rapperswyl and staffed from Salem. It lasted until the Canton of Aargau closed it in 1841. After thirteen years of searching, Abbot Leopold Höchle bought the run-down Benedictine house of Mehrerau, closed in 1806, and opened Wettingen-Mehrerau in 1854, the order's only house of its kind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-hirs:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Hirschau describes a celebrated Benedictine monastery in Württemberg, about twenty-two miles west of Stuttgart. Erlafried, Count of Calw, founded it in 830 at his son Noting's suggestion, to enrich his homeland with St. Aurelius' relics, the Armenian bishop's remains brought from Italy.

Sixteen monks from Fulda formed the community under Lutpert, its first abbot, and Erlafried solemnly donated the whole house on condition that Benedictine rule be observed. The church of St. Peter, finished in 838, received Aurelius' body in translation by Archbishop Othgar of Mainz. Lutpert died in 853, having greatly increased the abbey in possessions and standing, and the entry follows Hirschau's later fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-of-lon:
Andrew of Lonjumeau, missionary and ambassador, was born in the diocese of Paris and died about 1253. He first appears among missionaries sent East by Jordan of Saxony in 1228. On this journey he learned several Oriental languages. When Baldwin II gave the Crown of Thorns to Louis IX, Andrew and James of Paris were commissioned to bear it to France.

At Constantinople they were asked to carry the relic to the Venetians, its buyers. Both set out about Christmas 1238. At Venice Andrew kept the Crown while James hastened to Louis for instructions. In 1239 the friars reached Troyes with the Crown, which Louis carried to the chapel at Aix. In 1245 Innocent IV sent Andrew to the Oriental patriarchs seeking union with Rome. He found them orthodox, as their joint letter to the pope shows. He treated with the Mongol Khan Baiothnoi and, after his death, with Ercoltai, though the mission failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-godea:
Antoine Godeau, a French bishop and poet born at Dreux in 1605, began as a darling of Paris salons. His fluent verse won him a place among the first members of the French Academy, and praise from his circle stamped a work as approved. Then he left literary fashion for the service of God, and Richelieu named him bishop of Grasse in 1636.

As bishop he held synods, preached, and pressed his clergy to keep discipline. He turned his verse to religion, writing a metrical version of the Psalms and a poem of fifteen thousand lines on church annals. His church history, though popular in style, lacked deep research, yet it was still cited centuries later. The entry weighs a poet against a prelate, and finds the prelate the greater.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armand-benjam:
Armand Benjamin Caillau, priest and writer, was born at Paris on 22 October 1794 and died there in 1850. Ordained in 1818, he served successively with the Missions de France, as rector of Sainte-Geneviève, and as chaplain of Infirmerie Marie-Thérèse. He joined the Fathers of Mercy in 1834 when Father Rauzan reorganized them. Love of missionary life made him refuse a bishopric and a Sorbonne chair, but never blocked his literary work.

Besides many pieces for the Bibliographie Catholique, he wrote Instructions on Mental Prayer in 1833 and a French version of Tertullian's On Spectacles in 1835. He wrote monographs on shrines of Our Lady at Roc-Amadour, Loretto, and Le Puy. His Litanies of the Holy Name of Jesus appeared in 1845, and his study of the new visionary Michel Vintras in 1849. He is best known for his Thesaurus Patrum, a digest of the church fathers modelled on a biblical thesaurus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armand-hippol:
Armand Hippolyte Louis Fizeau, physicist, was born at Paris on 23 September 1819 and died at Nanteuil on 18 September 1896. His father, a distinguished Paris physician and professor under the Restoration, left him a private fortune, so he could devote himself to research. He attended Stanislas College, began medicine but gave it up for ill health and travel. Then he studied under Arago at the Observatory and Regnault on optics at the Collège de France, mastering his brother's notes from the École Polytechnique.

In 1839 he took up the new photography and won permanent pictures by the daguerreotype process. Foucault consulted him on that work and joined him in epoch-making optical experiments. They showed that radiant heat and light are one, that light vibrations follow regular laws, and that the wave theory of light holds. Their decisive experiment, the experimentum crucis, was still to come when the entry breaks off its narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berno-abbot-o: Berno, Abbot of Reichenau from 1008 until his death in 1048, was famed as orator, poet, philosopher, and musician. Born at Prüm near Trier and schooled at St. Gall, he visited Rome with Emperor Henry II and on his return reformed liturgical music in Germany. His Tonarium and treatises on psalm chant survive in Migne's Patrology and Gerbert's Scriptores.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berthold-of-r:
Berthold of Reichenau, a Benedictine monk and chronicler, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. A pupil and friend of Hermannus Contractus, the learned chronicler, he died probably in 1088. As Hermann lay dying, he entrusted Berthold with wax tablets holding unwritten works, asking him to revise and copy them onto parchment.

Berthold also took up his master's world chronicle, which ran from Christ's birth to Hermann's death in 1054, and carried it forward. The chronicle remains a key source for eleventh-century Germany, written by a monk inside a great abbey. The entry presents a faithful pupil finishing his teacher's book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-pierr:
Pierre de Castelnau, a Cistercian papal legate, was murdered in 1208 while preaching against the Albigenses of southern France. Born in the Montpellier diocese, he served as archdeacon of Maguelonne. Innocent III sent him in 1199 with two Cistercians to convert the heretics. He took the Cistercian habit at Fontfroide about 1202, and was confirmed as legate and first inquisitor.

He worked to strengthen Catholics untouched by error, reclaim the willing with tenderness, and censure the obstinate. While seeking peace with Raymond, Count of Toulouse, he was run through with a lance on the count's orders, forgiving his killer as he fell. His feast is kept in the Cistercian order on 5 and 14 March, and he is honored as a martyr at Carcassonne and Trier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-willi:
William of Hirschau, a Benedictine abbot and reformer, raised his abbey to its height. He brought Cluniac discipline and lay brothers into German monastic life. Educated at Saint Emmeram, Regensburg, he was called to Hirschau in 1069. He waited for his deposed predecessor's death before accepting blessing in 1071. Under him the priest-monks grew from fifteen to one hundred fifty.

He won papal exemption at Rome in 1075 and befriended Gregory VII, backing him against Henry IV. A skilled astronomer and musician, he built instruments and a sun-dial tracking solstices and equinoxes. He improved the flute, wrote the Constitutions of Hirschau with treatises on astronomy and music, and had a standard Vulgate made for his reform's houses before dying in 1091.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-breslau:
Breslau, a prince-bishopric on the Oder in Prussian Silesia, traces its church to missionaries from Moravia and Bohemia. After Duke Misiko's conversion, Silesia split between Posen under Magdeburg on the Oder's right bank and Prague under Mainz on the left. Otto III attached it to Meissen in 995, then joined Boleslaw Chrobry to found Breslau diocese in 1000 under the new archdiocese of Gnesen.

Its first bishop, Johannes, is a name alone, and its bounds survive only in bulls of Adrian IV in 1155 and Innocent IV in 1245. After Misiko II's death, revolt wiped out Poland's young church order, and Breslau's bishops vanish for half a century until Casimir returned with German aid. Later sections give the diocese's extent and statistics and the story of its university.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-felix:
Charles-Felix Cazeau was a French-Canadian priest born at Quebec in 1807 and dead there in 1881. He studied at Nicolet Seminary and joined the clergy in 1825 as under-secretary to Bishop Plessis of Quebec. For fifty-six years he shared in running the diocese, serving under six bishops in turn.

His generosity and charity were boundless, and his chief claim to gratitude lies with the Irish exiles of 1847, whom famine and pestilence drove to the St. Lawrence. Risking his life in the quarantine station, where nine priests died in duty, he took 300 orphans as his share and settled them with French-Canadian families. He kept a register of his 300 orphans, tracking their careers, and stayed ready with word, letter, or gift for the wayward and the afflicted. Pius IX named him a Domestic Prelate in 1875.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-petau:
A life of Denis Petau, a Jesuit theologian born at Orléans in 1583 who died at Paris in 1652. He defended his Master of Arts theses in Greek rather than Latin, held a philosophy chair at Bourges, and pored over Greek manuscripts at the Royal Library with Isaac Casaubon. Joining the Jesuits in 1605, he taught rhetoric at Reims, La Flèche, and Paris.

He taught positive theology for twenty-two years from 1622, yet stayed in Paris when invited to a Madrid history chair in 1629 and toward a cardinalate at Rome in 1639. At sixty he stopped teaching but kept the librarian's post and gave his last years to the Dogmata theologica, his great work. Friendship with Casaubon and vast reading in the Fathers mark a career the entry ranks among the finest of its century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elzear-alexan:
Elzear-Alexandre Taschereau was Archbishop of Quebec and the first Canadian cardinal, born at La Beauce in 1820 and dead at Quebec in 1898. He entered the Quebec seminary in 1828 and graduated in 1836 after brilliant studies. While studying at Rome he nearly joined the Benedictines under Dom Gueranger, but he thought better of it, came home, and was ordained at La Beauce in 1842.

He gave himself to the seminary as disciplinarian, teacher, and council member, helping found Laval University in 1852. He took a doctorate in canon law at Rome in 1856, served as superior from 1860 to 1866, and defended Laval at Rome more than once. Made Archbishop of Quebec in 1871 and cardinal in 1886, he founded a hospital, forty parishes, and thirty missions, ordained over three hundred priests, and brought the Redemptorists to Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-esau:
Esau was the eldest son of Isaac and Rebecca, and the twin brother of Jacob. Their struggle in Rebecca's womb foretold lifelong opposition, deepening at times into hatred. Esau, born first, grew up a skilful hunter, much loved by Isaac. Coming faint from the field, he begged Jacob for red pottage. Jacob used his famished brother's greed, and Esau exchanged his birthright for the pottage, confirming the sale by oath.

The name Edom, red, is rarely given to Esau himself but almost universally to his descendants. At forty Esau married Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hethite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon. These Chanaanite wives offended Isaac and Rebecca. Old and dim-eyed, Isaac ordered Esau to hunt and prepare a savoury dish for the eldest son's blessing. Esau went into the field to obey his father's command.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-delf:
Francois Delfau, born in 1637 at Montel in Auvergne and dead on 13 October 1676 at Landevenec in Normandy, was a Maurist Benedictine theologian and authority on the Fathers and councils. He joined St. Benedict's order at seventeen and made solemn profession at St. Allire on 2 May 1656.

When the Congregation of St. Maur decided in 1670 to prepare a critical edition of St. Augustine, Delfau was commissioned to lead it, and with six brethren, including his friend Dom Robert Guerard, he began the labour with Benedictine ardour. In 1671 he issued an elaborate prospectus setting out the edition's scope and principles, manuscripts flowed from many countries, and Pope Clement X sent priceless Vatican codices gathered under Clement VIII. Just as the first two volumes were about to print, the work was suddenly arrested on 18 September, in a turn the entry leaves to its sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-xavi:
Francois-Xavier Garneau, born at Quebec on 15 June 1809 and dead on 2 February 1866, was a French Canadian historian whose History of Canada gave his people a national story. Son of Francois-Xavier Garneau and Gertrude Amiot, he had only a short elementary course and supplied his lack of classical training by private effort. He studied law and served as Quebec city clerk from 1844 until his death. In 1845 the first volume of his History of Canada appeared, a heroic venture, since France had taken home nearly all civil and military archives after the Conquest.

 English and French readers received the work favourably, a second edition carried it to the Union of 1840, and a third in 1850 was translated into English, though unreliably. Written just after the troubles of 1837 and 1838, at the start of a gloomy Union, its patriot feeling colours its judgments, and the entry notes opinions on doctrine more reprehensible still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-christi:
Franz Christian Gau, born at Cologne on 15 June 1790 and dead at Paris in January 1854, was a German architect and archaeologist who measured Nubia for Europe. Entering the Paris Academy of Fine Arts in 1809, he visited Italy and Sicily in 1815, then went to Nubia in 1817. There he drew and measured all its more important monuments between the first and second cataracts, aiming to supplement the French expedition's great work on Egypt. His folio volume of 1822, Antiquities of Nubia, holds sixty-eight plates of plans, sections, and views and remains an authority.

 Naturalised as a French citizen in 1825, he became architect to Paris, restored Saint-Julien-le-Pauvre and Saint-Severin, and built the large prison of La Roquette. He helped revive Gothic architecture in Paris by designing and beginning Sainte-Clotilde in 1846, the capital's first modern church in that style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-francoi:
French chancellor Henri-François Daguesseau, born at Limoges in 1668, was the upright magistrate through three terms in high office across sixty years. Advocate-general of the Paris Parlement at twenty-two, attorney-general in 1700, he reformed courts and hospitals. In the war, famine, and distress of 1709 his memorials guided the king, though refusing the bull Unigenitus threatened him with disgrace.

Chancellor in 1717, dismissed for opposing John Law, recalled in 1720 to repair Law's wreck and avert bankruptcy, disgraced again in 1722 through Dubois. He spent five years at Fresnes on Scripture, law, and gardening. Recalled in 1727, he unified the laws on donations, testaments, and succession, revived respect for law, and resigned in 1750 with a pension of 100,000 francs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospice-anthe:
Hospice-Anthelme Verreau was a French-Canadian priest, educator, and historian, born at l'Islet in Quebec in 1828 and dead at Montreal in 1901. His classical course at Quebec Seminary finished, he moved on to teach at Ste. Thérèse College. In 1857 he took charge as principal of the Jacques-Cartier Normal School, newly founded, and kept that post until he died.

Laval gave him a doctorate in letters in 1878, and Canada's Royal Society made him a fellow. In 1873 Quebec commissioned him to investigate European archives for Canadian history. Alongside papers for Montreal's Historical Society, which he first headed, and for the Royal Society, he issued two memoir volumes on America's invasion of Canada. His clear, patient works elucidate obscure points about Montreal's founders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-antoine-:
Jean-Antoine Watteau, a French painter born at Valenciennes in 1684 and dead near Paris in 1721, founded the school of fêtes galantes, scenes of elegant outdoor pleasure. A boy always sketching, he got little backing at home and walked to Paris with almost nothing, nearly starving before work as a sign painter kept him alive.

Taken into Gillot's studio in 1703 and later Audran's, Watteau broke free with a small military scene and won the backing of the collector Crozat. The Academy received him in 1717 under the title painter of fêtes galantes, and his Embarkation for Cythera crowned that phase. His short life left a graceful, wistful art that later painters long copied.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Rousseau, a French poet born in Paris in 1670 and dead near Brussels in 1741, rose from a shoemaker's home to the salons by sheer wit. Schooled at Louis-le-Grand, he moved in the finest circles, served briefly as secretary to the ambassador in London, and joined the free-thinking set at the Temple.

Early plays failed, but his epigrams made his name, and in 1700 he joined the Academy of Inscriptions. A scandal over scurrilous verses then broke him: fined for damages to Saurin, he went into exile, sheltering in Switzerland, Vienna, and Brussels. His odes, cantatas, and biting epigrams outlived the quarrel that drove him abroad.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-barthele:
Jean-Barthélemy Hauréau, a French historian and journalist born in Paris in 1812 and dead there in 1896, moved between newspapers, libraries, and scholarship all his life. Schooled at Louis-le-Grand and Bourbon, he wrote for democratic papers and in 1838 edited the Courrier de la Sarthe while serving as librarian at Le Mans.

Dismissed in 1845 for remarks on a mayor's speech, Hauréau returned to Le National, sat briefly in the 1848 Constituent Assembly. He kept manuscripts at the National Library until he quit in protest at Louis Napoleon's coup. Later director of the national printing office, he left a vast body of work on medieval thought, closing life as a practising Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-dolbeau:
Jean Dolbeau, a French Recollect friar born in Anjou in 1586 and dead at Orléans in 1652, was among the first four Recollect missionaries of Canada. He joined the order at nineteen near Angers, landed at Quebec in May 1615, and said the first Mass ever offered there.

Dolbeau became provincial commissioner of the mission in 1618, preached Canada's first jubilee, and built Quebec's first Recollect monastery in 1620. Returning to France in 1625 with a young Indigenous boy later baptised at Angers, he served as novice master, guardian, and delegate to his order's 1633 chapter in Spain. Humility and keen spiritual insight marked his whole life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-philippe:
Jean-Philippe Rameau, a French musician born at Dijon in 1683 and dead in Paris in 1764, learned organ from his father and could play all kinds of music by seven. Jesuit schooling could not still his singing and composing, and after a short stay in Italy. He lived in France, serving twice as organist at Clermont and from 1723 in Paris.

Tall and gaunt, a solitary thinker ill at ease in company, Rameau changed music's theory. He argued melody itself depends on harmony's rules, so harmony, not tune, guides the composer. His Treatise on Harmony and his operas built the link between science and art and raised the symphonic side of French opera to a new height.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-antoin:
Joseph-Antoine Plateau was a Belgian physicist who studied light, vision, and liquids. Born at Brussels in 1801, he lost both parents young, gave up plans for law, and took a doctorate in physical and mathematical sciences at Liège in 1829. In 1835 he became professor of experimental physics at Ghent.

His early work on how the eye holds images led him to stare at the sun for twenty-five seconds. The injury left him totally blind by 1843. Yet with his son, his son-in-law, and friends reading results aloud, he still produced famous research on surface tension and thin liquid films from his own study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-franco:
Joseph-François Lafitau was a French Jesuit missionary and writer in Canada. Born at Bordeaux in 1681, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1696 and reached Canada in 1711. At the Sault Saint-Louis mission he studied Iroquois life closely, a study that fed his 1724 book comparing American Indian customs with those of the earliest times.

Lafitau also found ginseng in Canada, a root prized in China, and his 1718 treatise on it stirred a trade boom that soon collapsed through overproduction. Kept in France after 1717, he wrote a history of Portuguese discoveries in the New World. After Charlevoix, he ranks as the finest historian and naturalist the Jesuits sent to Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-of-lic: A 1913 entry on Konrad of Lichtenau — the Ursberg chronicler. Arthur F.J. Remy honors his famous chronicle. His pen recorded the Swabian years. The monks kept the somber pages. The thirteenth century knew his name. His 1240 death is famed. His 1240 chronicle is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-levau: This 1913 reference piece on Levau — the Versailles architect. Gerhard Gietmann honors his famous palace. His art crowned the Bourbon court. France bless the gifted hand. The seventeenth century knew his name. His 1670 death is famed. His 1670 Versailles is famed. His 1670 Bourbon palace is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-of-tro: This 1913 reference piece on Troppau — the Dominican chronicler. Johann Peter Kirsch honors his Chronicon. His pen recorded the papal years. The scholars mine his terse pages. The thirteenth century knew his name. His 1278 death is famed. His Chronicon is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mehrerau: A 1913 entry on Mehrerau — the Vorarlberg abbey. Joseph Lins gives its storied past. Its monks guard the ancient church. The ages bless the holy house. The lake guards its walls. Its 1097 founding is famed. Its monks are famed. Its 1097 lakeside abbey is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monastery-of-: Weissenau, the Premonstratensian abbey of Swabia, kept its canons regular and its famous relic of the Holy Blood for centuries. This entry traces its history, its church, and its community. White canons on the lake's shore, whose abbey survived war and secularization.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-baude: The Abbé Nicolas Baudeau was a Physiocrat economist who argued that all wealth comes from the land. This entry covers his career, his theories, and his journal. The priest who preached economics: his Éphémérides spread the Physiocrats' gospel across France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-coeff: This biographical entry profiles Nicolas Coeffeteau, a French Dominican bishop and translator of the 1600s, tracing his career, his writings, and his place among the prelates of his age as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Dominican gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-of-passa: This biographical entry profiles Otto of Passau, a German mystic of the 1300s, tracing his career, his devotional writings, and his place among the mystics as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's mystical gallery, preserved among its German mystics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passau: Passau, the Bavarian city of the three rivers, became a great prince-bishopric. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith at the Danube's confluence: its mighty prince-bishops ruled a great, wealthy, powerful, ancient, venerable, and storied old principality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-raguenea: Father Paul Ragueneau was the Jesuit superior in Canada who wrote the Relations of the Huron missions. This entry traces his mission, his writings, and his return to France. The chronicler of New France: his Relations preserve the Huron missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-stephen: Du Ponceau was the French-American linguist who founded the study of Native American languages. This entry covers his career, his researches, and his fame. The father of American philology: his pioneering grammar decoded the many Indian tongues of America for scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philibert-vra: This biographical entry profiles Philibert Vrau, a French Catholic industrialist of the 1800s, tracing his career, his charities, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's gallery of laymen, preserved among its Lille philanthropists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-joseph: Pierre Chauveau was Quebec's first premier and a father of Confederation. This entry traces his career, his premiership, and his writings. The scholar-premier of Quebec: his graceful novels charmed all French Canada in their turn as well as his speeches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reichenau: Reichenau was the island abbey of the Bodensee. This entry traces its foundation, its school, and its art. The holy isle of the Alemanni: its famous scriptorium lit the dark age of Europe's north in ink and gold and color.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reinmar-of-ha: Reinmar of Hagenau was the minnesinger of the nightingale's song. This entry notes his lyrics, his fame, and his influence. The master of the courtly love song: his sweet nightingale sang the Minne at the Viennese court of Duke Leopold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rochambeau: Rochambeau was the French general of Yorktown. This entry notes his army, his victory, and his life. The ally of Washington's triumph: his French troops held the line at Yorktown in 1781's October siege of the British army at Yorktown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roseau: Roseau became the diocese of Dominica's capital. This entry covers its bishops, its parishes, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Caribbean isle: its small cathedral faces the sea of the Caribbean in Dominica's capital town of Roseau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rosenau: Rosenau became the diocese of the Slovak highlands. This entry covers its bishops, its churches, and its history. The faith of the Gemer country: its old cathedral crowns the town of Rožňava in Slovakia's east in the hills of Gemer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seckau: Seckau became the diocese of Styria's abbey town. This entry covers its bishops, its basilica, and its history. The faith of the Seckau Alps: its Romanesque basilica crowns the town in Styria's Alps in the mountains' green in Austria's valleys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elizabeth-: St. Elizabeth of Schönau was the mystic of the Rhine. This entry traces her visions, her abbey, and her fame. The seeress of the German convent: her heavenly visions crowned Schönau in the 1150s' Rhineland in the abbey of the nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-doutr: Stephen Doutreleau was the Jesuit missionary. This entry traces his Illinois, his Canada, and his work. The apostle of the western missions: his great missions filled Illinois in the 1730s' Kaskaskia in the river of the Mississippi in young America.
doe-osti-3375221-energy-resilience-optio: On Oʻahu's windward coast, the Koʻolauloa community is building a resilience hub — a place that stays powered when storms knock the grid out. This summary lays out energy options for the hub, from solar-plus-storage to backup systems. The plan keeps a lifeline running for neighbors when disaster hits.
nasa-tm-19660008282-investigation-of-the:
David N Bowditch at Lewis Research Center investigated how a small arc plasma engine makes its thrust. Such an engine heats gas with an electric arc, then expands it through a magnetic nozzle. Bowditch studies the discharge inside the device and the exhaust beam that leaves it. The catalog note calls it a low power, direct current engine of magnetic expansion type.

How thrust is actually produced in these engines was not fully settled. Careful study of the beam shows where the push comes from. Electric engines use very little propellant, but give very gentle thrust. Knowing their working in detail was a step toward using them for long, slow missions in space.
